opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those questions where I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know, and people are often more confident than they should be in either direction.

The standard framing is: you take an image of a panda, change some pixels by an amount a human can't even perceive, and suddenly the model is 99% sure it's a gibbon. Humans clearly don't work like that, so the conclusion people draw is that neural networks are fundamentally broken in some way that humans aren't. And I think there's something real there. But I also think the comparison is a lot less fair than it looks.

When I attack a neural network, I have complete white-box access. I can compute gradients. I can query it millions of times. I know every weight. I can run an optimization procedure that searches for the single worst-case input in a huge space. We have never been able to do anything remotely like that to a human visual system. So when people say "humans are robust to adversarial examples," what they really mean is "humans are robust to the adversarial examples we've constructed for neural networks," which is a very different claim. It's entirely possible that if you had gradient access to a human brain, you could find some weird input that makes a person confidently see a cat where there's a dog. We just can't run that experiment.

And we do have hints in that direction. Optical illusions are, in a sense, naturally occurring adversarial examples for human vision. They're found by a much weaker search process, just people noticing things over centuries, and yet they still reliably fool essentially everyone. There's also some work showing that adversarial examples that transfer across many models can slightly bias human judgments when people only see the image very briefly. That's not proof humans are as fragile as neural nets, but it should make us a bit humble.

That said, I don't want to fully explain the gap away. There do seem to be real differences. Models trained the standard way pick up on features that are genuinely predictive in the data but that humans would consider meaningless, high-frequency texture patterns and so on. They're doing exactly what we asked: minimize loss on the training distribution. Nothing in that objective says "be invariant to tiny perturbations." Humans, on the other hand, have been shaped by evolution in a world with actual adversaries, predators trying to camouflage, prey trying to look like something else, so there was real pressure for a kind of robustness that our training objectives just don't impose.

And the practical reality is that a decade of work on adversarial robustness has been pretty humbling. We've made progress, adversarial training works to a degree, but robust accuracy on something like ImageNet under fairly small perturbations is still far below clean accuracy. Most of the defenses that were proposed turned out to be broken when evaluated properly. So whatever the theoretical story about humans is, the empirical fact is that we don't know how to build models that are robust in the way we'd want.

The reason this matters more now than it did a few years ago is that we're deploying language models and agents into settings where there are real adversaries. Prompt injection, jailbreaks, these are adversarial examples in a new domain, and they have the same flavor: the model does something no reasonable human would do in response to an input a human would find obviously suspicious. Whether or not humans would also break under a sufficiently powerful attack, the attacks we can actually run against models today work, and they work cheaply. So I think the right takeaway is less "neural nets are fundamentally different from brains" and more "we should assume these systems can be manipulated and design everything around them accordingly."

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd push back on a little bit is the premise that the gap is as large as it looks. There's been a fair amount of work showing that humans are also fooled by adversarial examples, at least under some conditions. If you take an image that's been perturbed to fool a model and flash it to a person for a very short time, say tens of milliseconds, people's classifications shift in the direction the attack intended. So the robustness we have isn't magic. It seems to be that we get to look at things for longer, we integrate over time, we move our eyes around, and we have a lot of context and priors that the network just doesn't get in a single forward pass. If you constrain humans to something closer to what the model is being asked to do, the gap shrinks.

That said, I don't want to overstate that either, because there's still clearly a real gap. If I take a picture of a cat and I add a perturbation that no human can even perceive, and the model is now extremely confident it's guacamole, that's not something that's going to happen to a person no matter how long they look at it. So what's going on there?

My honest answer is that I don't think anybody fully knows, but there are a couple of explanations I find somewhat compelling. One is that these models are just trained on the wrong objective for the thing we want. We train them to minimize loss on the training distribution, and the training distribution has essentially zero mass on adversarially perturbed inputs. So the model is free to use whatever features happen to be predictive, and it turns out a lot of the most predictive features are these high-frequency, brittle things that humans don't use at all. There was a nice paper framing this as "adversarial examples are features, not bugs," and I think that's a big part of the story. The model isn't wrong, in a sense. It's picked up on real statistical regularities in the data. They're just regularities we don't care about and that an adversary can manipulate very cheaply.

The second piece is dimensionality. Images are high dimensional, and in a high-dimensional space, if the decision boundary is even slightly off from where it should be in most directions, you can accumulate a lot of small errors into one large change in output with a tiny change in input. Humans may be doing something closer to a much lower-dimensional representation, where there just aren't that many directions available to exploit.

And then the third thing I'd say, which is a bit more pessimistic, is that we've now spent close to a decade trying to close this gap, and the only thing that reliably works is adversarial training, where you literally show the model the attacks during training. That gets you some robustness, at a cost in clean accuracy, and only against the specific threat model you trained for. If you change the perturbation type, the robustness mostly goes away. That tells me we haven't found the right inductive bias. We've found a patch. If humans are robust because of something architectural or because of how we learn, we haven't figured out what that thing is yet.

So where I land is: the gap is partly an artifact of comparing a human with full context and time against a model with one shot, partly that we're training models to care about things humans don't, and partly a genuine open problem that I'd be lying if I said I knew how to solve.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the gap is real, and part of it is that we’re not making quite the same comparison. With a neural network, we can specify exactly what it means to make a mistake, and then run an optimization procedure to find an input that causes that mistake. We don’t have that kind of access to a human brain. So our ability to find adversarial examples for the two systems is very different.

But there is still something striking about taking an image that a person recognizes perfectly well, changing it by an amount they can’t perceive, and getting a model to confidently say it’s something else. That suggests the model’s decision depends on features that don’t line up with the features we use, even when its accuracy on ordinary images is very good.

Humans also make mistakes on carefully constructed inputs—optical illusions are an obvious example—but I’d be cautious about treating those as exactly the same phenomenon. The constraints matter. Is the change invisible? Does the mistake persist if you look again? What information does the attacker have?

So I wouldn’t conclude that humans are universally robust and neural networks aren’t. I’d say ordinary test accuracy tells us much less about robustness than we might have hoped, and understanding the human comparison requires being precise about what we’re testing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things tangled up here. One is that neural networks really do fail in ways that seem very strange to us. You can take an image that a model classifies correctly, make a tiny change, and cause it to give a completely different answer with high confidence. That's a real phenomenon that we should understand.

But the other question is whether humans are actually robust in the sense that we're asking the neural network to be robust. Usually, when we attack a neural network, we give the attacker access to the model and let them optimize an input specifically to make it fail. When we test a human, we typically show them that same image. The fact that the human gets it right tells us that the attack doesn't transfer to the human. It doesn't necessarily tell us that you couldn't construct a different attack against the human.

Humans have optical illusions, and we make mistakes under time pressure or when images are presented in unusual ways. Those aren't necessarily the same thing as a small, adversarial perturbation, so I wouldn't claim that they settle the question either. The challenge is making the comparison fair: what information does the attacker have, what changes can they make, and how much time does the person or model have to respond?

So I think there is a meaningful gap, particularly for those tiny changes to otherwise ordinary images. But I would be careful about jumping from that observation to the conclusion that humans have some general robustness property that neural networks fundamentally lack.
